shadecast · measured result · 39 plans, 3 cities

Same money, opposite plans

Every plan below was simulated with real physics. Across three cities on three continents, how you arrange trees matters more than where you put them, and the two standard objectives disagree about what to do.

Plans 39, all engine-simulated Cities Ahmedabad, Lagos, Rio Budgets $0.4M to $18.3M Physics SOLWEIG at 1 m

The trade-off, every plan

Each curve is one arrangement traced from the smallest budget to the largest. Right is more cooling; up is more people pushed below the 45 C danger threshold. If the two objectives agreed, the curves would sit on top of each other.

horizontal: mean exposure drop (C)  ·  vertical: people moved below 45 C  ·  hover any point for its budget

clustered, what greedy produces scattered corridor, along streets

What the curves say

Ahmedabad: the curves cross. Clustered climbs steeply upward and barely rightward; scattered does the reverse. The two objectives pick opposite plans.

Lagos: scattered dominates on both axes. No conflict, because 86% of residents are already above the threshold, so spreading cooling thin still reaches them.

Rio: the curves nearly coincide on people but separate sharply on exposure. Rio already has 19.5% canopy and 45 m buildings, so it is in the saturation regime and every plan buys less.

Arrangement beats targeting, in every city

Greedy plants where it is hottest. Hot ground is contiguous, so greedy produces a clustered plan by construction. Clustered trees then shade ground that is already shaded: the interaction between nearby interventions is saturation, not synergy.

The equity finding, now across three cities

Lagos returns 6x more cooling per dollar than Rio. The treeless, dense, low-rise city has by far the highest return, and the leafy high-rise city the lowest. That points adaptation money in the opposite direction to where it currently goes.
